title: Smart Salary Sacrifice: Turn Your Hourly Rate into Annual, Fortnightly, and Tax-Smart Pay
description: Learn how to convert your hourly rate to annual, fortnightly, and weekly pay using a 38-hour week. Includes tax, super, and smart salary sacrifice tips from Fair Work and ATO.
salarySummary: For a 38-hour week, annual gross pay is your hourly rate × 38 × 52, with super paid on top and tax calculated on the 2026–27 resident scale.

faqs.q: What is smart salary sacrifice and how does it affect my take-home pay?
faqs.a: Smart salary sacrifice (also called salary packaging) lets you use part of your pre-tax salary to pay for approved benefits like a car, phone, or extra super contributions. This reduces your taxable income, so you may pay less income tax and Medicare levy. However, your employer may need to pay fringe benefits tax (FBT) on some benefits, which can limit what’s offered. For most employees, sacrificing into super is a common strategy – your super fund taxes those contributions at 15% instead of your marginal rate. Always check with your employer and consider professional tax advice, as the benefits depend on your income and the package offered.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then by 52. For a standard full-time role of 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52 = annual gross pay. For example, at the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour (from 1 July 2026), the annual gross is $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,261.44. This assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. Your actual pay may differ if you work different hours or have an enterprise agreement.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage, award rates, and casual loading?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage is the base minimum for all employees not covered by an award or agreement – from 1 July 2026 it is $26.44 per hour. Award rates are higher minimums set by the Fair Work Commission for specific industries and occupations, and they include penalty rates and allowances. Casual loading is an extra 25% on top of the base rate for casual employees, compensating for lack of paid leave. For example, a casual on the National Minimum Wage gets $33.05 per hour ($26.44 + 25%). Super is paid on top of these rates at 12% of ordinary earnings.

bodyMarkdown:
## From Hourly to Annual: The 38-Hour Week Formula

If you’re paid by the hour or considering a salary offer, knowing how your hourly rate translates into annual, fortnightly, and weekly pay is essential. The standard full-time working week in Australia is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. To estimate your annual gross pay, use this simple formula:

**Hourly rate × hours per week × 52 = annual gross pay**

For a 38-hour week, that’s **hourly rate × 38 × 52**. This assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. It’s a starting point for budgeting and comparing job offers.

### Example: National Minimum Wage

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour. For a full-time employee working 38 hours:

- Annual gross: $26.44 × 38 × 52 = **$52,261.44**
- Weekly: $26.44 × 38 = **$1,004.72** (rounded from $1,004.9 per the Fair Work Ombudsman)
- Fortnightly: weekly × 2 = **$2,009.44**

If you’re a casual employee, you receive a 25% loading on top of the base rate. That’s $33.05 per hour, giving an annual gross of **$65,326.80** for 38 hours per week. Remember, super is paid on top of these amounts.

### Award Rates vs. Minimum Wage

Many employees are covered by an award that sets higher minimum rates than the National Minimum Wage. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) for each award, listing minimum pay rates, allowances, and penalty rates. Always check your award or enterprise agreement, as it may have different classifications and overtime rules. The formula still applies: hourly rate × 38 × 52, but your actual rate may be higher.

## From Annual to Fortnightly and Weekly

Once you have your annual gross, you can break it down:

- **Weekly**: annual ÷ 52
- **Fortnightly**: weekly × 2 (or annual ÷ 26)
- **Monthly**: annual ÷ 12 (but note that monthly pay cycles often vary)

For example, the average full-time adult ordinary time earnings (from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, May 2026) are $2,083.70 per week. That’s an annual gross of about $108,352.40. A fortnightly pay would be $4,167.40.

## Tax and Medicare Levy

Your take-home pay depends on income tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15%
- $45,001 – $135,000: 30%
- $135,001 – $190,000: 37%
- $190,001+: 45%

Plus a Medicare levy of generally 2% of taxable income. The tax-free threshold means the first $18,200 is tax-free. Our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator uses these rates and the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds for Medicare (since the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of this reference).

**Example**: For a gross annual salary of $80,000 (about $40.48 per hour for 38 hours), the estimated tax (including Medicare) would be around $16,567, leaving a take-home of about $63,433 per year, or $1,219.87 per week.

## Superannuation: Paid on Top

Under the super guarantee, your employer must pay 12% of your ordinary earnings into your super fund. This is on top of your salary, not deducted from it. From 1 July 2026, employers must pay super each payday (Payday Super), and contributions must be received by your fund within 7 business days.

Super is calculated on your ordinary time earnings (usually your base hourly rate × hours worked, excluding overtime). There is a maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year – earnings above that don’t attract compulsory super.

For the National Minimum Wage example ($52,261.44), the employer’s super contribution would be 12% × $52,261.44 = **$6,271.37** per year, paid into your super fund.

## Smart Salary Sacrifice: A Tax-Effective Strategy

[Smart salary sacrifice](/topics/super-and-packaging) (also called salary packaging) allows you to use part of your pre-tax salary to pay for approved benefits, such as a car, laptop, or additional super contributions. By reducing your taxable income, you may pay less income tax and Medicare levy. However, your employer may need to pay fringe benefits tax (FBT) on some benefits, which can affect what’s offered.

### How It Works

Suppose you earn $100,000 per year. You could salary sacrifice $15,000 for a car, reducing your taxable income to $85,000. You’d pay tax on $85,000 instead of $100,000, potentially saving thousands. But your employer pays FBT on the car benefit, so not all employers offer this.

### Salary Sacrifice into Super

A common and tax-effective option is sacrificing into super. Your super fund taxes these contributions at 15% (instead of your marginal rate), and they count towards your concessional contribution cap of $32,500 per year (including your employer’s 12% contributions). Going over the cap may incur extra tax.

### Not-for-Profit Concessions

Some not-for-profit organisations receive FBT concessions or exemptions, making salary packaging more attractive for their employees. For example, you might package a car or school fees without your employer paying FBT.

### Important Changes

From 1 April 2027, work-related items (like laptops and phones) provided through a salary sacrifice arrangement will no longer be exempt from FBT. Always check current rules with the Australian Taxation Office.

## Putting It All Together: A Practical Example

Let’s say you’re offered a job at $45 per hour, 38 hours per week, as a permanent employee.

- Annual gross: $45 × 38 × 52 = **$88,920**
- Weekly: $1,710
- Fortnightly: $3,420
- Super (12% on top): $10,670.40 per year
- Estimated tax (2026–27, including Medicare): about $20,347, leaving take-home of **$68,573** per year ($1,318.71 per week)

If you choose smart salary sacrifice into super of $5,000 per year, your taxable income drops to $83,920, saving you about $1,500 in tax (at the 30% marginal rate). Your super gets an extra $5,000 (taxed at 15%), boosting your retirement savings.

## Important Notes and Limitations

This guide provides estimates. Your actual pay may differ due to:
- Unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances
- Salary sacrifice arrangements not included in the basic formula
- HELP or other loan repayments
- Medicare levy surcharge if you don’t have appropriate private hospital cover

Always refer to the Fair Work Ombudsman for your award or agreement, and the Australian Taxation Office for tax and super obligations. Use our [reference tables](/data) for up-to-date rates.

### Disclaimer

Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.
